claim: Kinesin is part of a cytoskeletal motor family that moves cellular cargoes primarily to the cell periphery (microtubule plus end).
source: Kinesin is part of a cytoskeletal motor family that moves cellular cargoes primarily to the cell periphery (microtubule plus end).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about kinesin function.

claim: Kinesin is important in key cellular processes like cell division and signaling.
source: It is important in key cellular processes like cell division and signaling (Gross et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gross et al., 2002.

claim: Kinesin is implicated in several neurological disorders.
source: It is also implicated in several neurological disorders (McLaughlin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to McLaughlin et al., 2016.

claim: Kinesin-1 moves 8.4 nm per ATP consumed.
source: For example, kinesin-1, the prototypical kinesin, moves 8.4 nm per ATP consumed, in a hand-over-hand motion, walking about 100 steps before detaching and traveling at a speed of ~0.77 μm/sec in vitro (Cai et al., 2007), and equal- or higher speed in vivo (Block et al., 1990; Stamer et al., 2002; Yildiz et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cai et al., 2007.

claim: Kinesin-1 walks in a hand-over-hand motion.
source: For example, kinesin-1, the prototypical kinesin, moves 8.4 nm per ATP consumed, in a hand-over-hand motion, walking about 100 steps before detaching and traveling at a speed of ~0.77 μm/sec in vitro (Cai et al., 2007), and equal- or higher speed in vivo (Block et al., 1990; Stamer et al., 2002; Yildiz et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cai et al., 2007.

claim: Kinesin-1 walks about 100 steps before detaching.
source: For example, kinesin-1, the prototypical kinesin, moves 8.4 nm per ATP consumed, in a hand-over-hand motion, walking about 100 steps before detaching and traveling at a speed of ~0.77 μm/sec in vitro (Cai et al., 2007), and equal- or higher speed in vivo (Block et al., 1990; Stamer et al., 2002; Yildiz et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cai et al., 2007.

claim: Kinesin-1 travels at a speed of ~0.77 μm/sec in vitro.
source: For example, kinesin-1, the prototypical kinesin, moves 8.4 nm per ATP consumed, in a hand-over-hand motion, walking about 100 steps before detaching and traveling at a speed of ~0.77 μm/sec in vitro (Cai et al., 2007), and equal- or higher speed in vivo (Block et al., 1990; Stamer et al., 2002; Yildiz et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cai et al., 2007.

claim: Kinesin-1 travels at equal or higher speed in vivo compared to in vitro.
source: For example, kinesin-1, the prototypical kinesin, moves 8.4 nm per ATP consumed, in a hand-over-hand motion, walking about 100 steps before detaching and traveling at a speed of ~0.77 μm/sec in vitro (Cai et al., 2007), and equal- or higher speed in vivo (Block et al., 1990; Stamer et al., 2002; Yildiz et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Block et al., 1990; Stamer et al., 2002; Yildiz et al., 2004.

claim: A single kinesin exerts up to ~6 pN force.
source: A single kinesin also exerts up to ~6 pN force (Svoboda and Block, 1994), and importantly, has an asymmetric run-length and velocity with regard to the direction of force on the microtubule (Figure 1A) (Coppin et al., 2002; Milic et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Svoboda and Block, 1994.

claim: A single kinesin has an asymmetric run-length and velocity with regard to the direction of force on the microtubule.
source: A single kinesin also exerts up to ~6 pN force (Svoboda and Block, 1994), and importantly, has an asymmetric run-length and velocity with regard to the direction of force on the microtubule (Figure 1A) (Coppin et al., 2002; Milic et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coppin et al., 2002; Milic et al., 2014 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: A cell is extremely dense, filled with proteins (~300 mg/ml), and only 60–80% water volume.
source: However, a cell is extremely dense, filled with proteins (~300 mg/ml), and only 60–80% water volume (Albe et al., 1990), resulting in a high viscosity and elastic modulus (Berret, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Albe et al., 1990.

claim: The high protein density in cells results in a high viscosity and elastic modulus.
source: However, a cell is extremely dense, filled with proteins (~300 mg/ml), and only 60–80% water volume (Albe et al., 1990), resulting in a high viscosity and elastic modulus (Berret, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Berret, 2016.

claim: Large cargos move at virtually the same rate in cells as in a water-based in-vitro environment.
source: Despite this, large cargos move at virtually the same rate as in a water-based in-vitro environment (Furuta et al., 2013; Howard et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Furuta et al., 2013; Howard et al., 1989.

claim: Multiple motors acting on a single cargo enable large cargos to move at the same rate in dense cellular environments as in vitro.
source: How is this possible? We argue that it is due to the action of multiple motors acting on a single cargo.
evidence: This is the authors' argument/hypothesis based on their reasoning.

claim: Electron microscopy shows that ~1 to 7 motors are bound to cellular cargoes.
source: Electron microscopy shows that ~1 to 7 motors are bound to cellular cargoes (Gross et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gross et al., 2007.

claim: Motors are inter-dependent such that the impairment of one motor type (e.g. dynein) causes severe impairment in the other (e.g. kinesin).
source: Motors are inter-dependent (Gross et al., 2002), such that the impairment of one motor type (e.g. dynein) causes severe impairment in the other (e.g. kinesin) (Gross et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gross et al., 2002.

claim: Run length and stall forces are typically greater for multiple vs single motor, although not necessarily in proportion.
source: Run length and stall forces are typically greater for multiple vs single motor, although not necessarily in proportion (Holzbaur and Goldman, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holzbaur and Goldman, 2010.

claim: Theoretical studies predict tension between multiple motors carrying the same cargo.
source: Theoretical studies predict tension between multiple motors carrying the same cargo (Arpağ et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arpağ et al., 2014.

claim: Tension between motors allows for their ability to efficiently bypass roadblocks.
source: This tension, we argue, allows for their ability to efficiently bypass roadblocks, which has yet to be shown experimentally.
evidence: This is the authors' argument, noting that experimental evidence is lacking.

claim: The Block group found an asymmetry when studying the run length of single kinesin as a function of force in an optical trap.
source: The Block group found an asymmetry when studying the run length of single kinesin as a function of force in an optical trap (Milic et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Milic et al., 2014 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The run length is greater for driving kinesin (50 nm at −6 pN rising rapidly to 1100 nm at 0 pN) vs. resisting kinesin (~100 nm at 2 pN slowly falling to 10 nm at 20 pN).
source: They found that the run length is greater for driving kinesin (50 nm at −6 pN rising rapidly to 1100 nm at 0 pN) vs. resisting kinesin (~100 nm at 2 pN slowly falling to 10 nm at 20 pN) (Figure 1A) (Milic et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Milic et al., 2014 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The Vale group saw kinesin velocity to be slower for driving-kinesin than resisting-kinesin.
source: Similarly, the Vale group saw kinesin velocity to be slower for driving-kinesin than resisting-kinesin (Figure 1B) (Coppin et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coppin et al., 2002 and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: One simulation showed that the asymmetric property of single kinesin under load leads to an average of one-third of kinesin's resisting in multi-motor situation.
source: One simulation showed that the asymmetric property of single kinesin under load leads to an average of one-third of kinesin's resisting in multi-motor situation (Arpağ et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arpağ et al., 2014.

claim: Simulations showed that the tension was between 0 to 15 pN between the kinesins carrying the cargo.
source: In addition, the tension was between 0 to 15 pN between the kinesins carrying the cargo (Arpağ et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arpağ et al., 2014.

claim: Simulations showed that force-dependent detachment of motors, particularly the resisting motors, is important for cargo speed.
source: Other simulations showed that, on a single cargo being driven by multiple motors, force-dependent detachment of motors (Arpağ et al., 2014), particularly the resisting motors (Nelson et al., 2014), is important for cargo speed.
evidence: Supported by citations to Arpağ et al., 2014 and Nelson et al., 2014.

claim: A number of experimental studies found negative cooperativity of kinesin.
source: A number of experimental studies found negative cooperativity of kinesin (Furuta et al., 2013; Jamison et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Furuta et al., 2013; Jamison et al., 2010.

claim: Multiple kinesins induce tension (up to 4 pN) on the cargo.
source: Through an in vitro force-gliding assay, which involves measuring nanometer displacement and piconewtons of force, we show that multiple mammalian kinesin-1 (from 2 to 8) communicate in a team by inducing tension (up to 4 pN) on the cargo.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experimental data.

claim: Kinesins adopt two distinct states, with one-third slowing down the microtubule and two-thirds speeding it up.
source: Kinesins adopt two distinct states, with one-third slowing down the microtubule and two-thirds speeding it up.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experimental data.

claim: Resisting kinesins tend to come off more rapidly than driving kinesins.
source: Resisting kinesins tend to come off more rapidly than, and speed up when pulled by driving kinesins, implying an asymmetric tug-of-war.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experimental data.

claim: Resisting kinesins speed up when pulled by driving kinesins.
source: Resisting kinesins tend to come off more rapidly than, and speed up when pulled by driving kinesins, implying an asymmetric tug-of-war.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experimental data.

claim: Multiple kinesins acting as a team implies an asymmetric tug-of-war.
source: Resisting kinesins tend to come off more rapidly than, and speed up when pulled by driving kinesins, implying an asymmetric tug-of-war.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Kinesins dynamically interact to overcome roadblocks, occasionally combining their forces.
source: Furthermore, kinesins dynamically interact to overcome roadblocks, occasionally combining their forces.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the authors' experimental data.

claim: Multiple kinesins acting as a team may play a significant role in facilitating smooth cargo motion in a dense environment.
source: Consequently, multiple kinesins acting as a team may play a significant role in facilitating smooth cargo motion in a dense environment.
evidence: This is an inference/conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Each kinesin was labeled with a quantum dot (QD) at a ratio of 1:1.
source: Each kinesin was labeled with a quantum dot (QD) at a ratio of 1:1, and attached by a 1565-base pair dsDNA molecule, which acts like a non-linear spring, to a non-stick polyethylene-glycol (PEG) coverslip.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Kinesin was attached by a 1565-base pair dsDNA molecule to a non-stick polyethylene-glycol (PEG) coverslip.
source: Each kinesin was labeled with a quantum dot (QD) at a ratio of 1:1, and attached by a 1565-base pair dsDNA molecule, which acts like a non-linear spring, to a non-stick polyethylene-glycol (PEG) coverslip.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: The 1565-base pair dsDNA molecule acts like a non-linear spring.
source: Each kinesin was labeled with a quantum dot (QD) at a ratio of 1:1, and attached by a 1565-base pair dsDNA molecule, which acts like a non-linear spring, to a non-stick polyethylene-glycol (PEG) coverslip.
evidence: This is a characterization of the DNA linker's mechanical properties.

claim: Driving kinesin stays attached to microtubule for an average of 3.0 ± 0.21 s.
source: With multiple kinesins, Figure 3A shows that driving kinesin stays attached to microtubule for an average of 3.0 ± 0.21 s, compared to 2.15 ± 0.15 s for resisting kinesin.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Resisting kinesin stays attached to microtubule for an average of 2.15 ± 0.15 s.
source: With multiple kinesins, Figure 3A shows that driving kinesin stays attached to microtubule for an average of 3.0 ± 0.21 s, compared to 2.15 ± 0.15 s for resisting kinesin.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The average run length of driving-kinesin is 2.31 ± 0.18 µm.
source: Figure 3B shows that the average run length of driving-kinesin is 2.31 ± 0.18 µm, compared to 1.42 ± 0.09 µm for resisting kinesin.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The average run length of resisting kinesin is 1.42 ± 0.09 µm.
source: Figure 3B shows that the average run length of driving-kinesin is 2.31 ± 0.18 µm, compared to 1.42 ± 0.09 µm for resisting kinesin.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The asymmetry in run length and duration suggests there is tension between driving and resisting kinesins with multiple motors driving a single cargo.
source: Our observation of asymmetry in run length and duration suggests there is tension between driving and resisting kinesins with multiple motors driving a single (microtubule) cargo.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The tension between kinesins is estimated to be between 0 and 4 pN.
source: After 0.8 s, the tension increases and stays between below ~4 pN until kinesin detaches. Therefore, we estimate the tension between kinesins to be between 0 and 4 pN.
evidence: This is based on force calculations from experimental data using the eWLC model.

claim: There is a constant fraction—about 2/3—of kinesins which are driving.
source: Indeed, we found that there is a constant fraction—about 2/3—of kinesins which are driving.
evidence: This is experimental data from the force-gliding assay.

claim: About 1/3 of the kinesins are resisting, regardless of the total number of kinesins (from 1 to 8) attached to the microtubule.
source: This means that about 1/3 of the kinesins are resisting, regardless of the total number of kinesins (from 1 to 8) attached to the microtubule (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Driving kinesins slow down to match the cargo (microtubule) rate.
source: We find that for multiple kinesins, the driving kinesins slow down to match the cargo (microtubule) rate, and the resisting kinesins speed up to match the cargo (microtubule) rate.
evidence: This is experimental observation from the force-gliding assay.

claim: Resisting kinesins speed up to match the cargo (microtubule) rate.
source: We find that for multiple kinesins, the driving kinesins slow down to match the cargo (microtubule) rate, and the resisting kinesins speed up to match the cargo (microtubule) rate.
evidence: This is experimental observation from the force-gliding assay.

claim: The driving kinesins start at a velocity of ~1200 nm/s relative to microtubule.
source: On average, the driving kinesins start at a velocity of ~1200 nm/s and resisting kinesins at ~500 nm/s relative to microtubule (=absolute velocity of the microtubule minus absolute velocity of the kinesin) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is experimental data from velocity analysis.

claim: Resisting kinesins start at a velocity of ~500 nm/s relative to microtubule.
source: On average, the driving kinesins start at a velocity of ~1200 nm/s and resisting kinesins at ~500 nm/s relative to microtubule (=absolute velocity of the microtubule minus absolute velocity of the kinesin) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is experimental data from velocity analysis.

claim: Driving kinesins slow down and resisting kinesins speed up to ~830 nm/s, which is the average microtubule velocity.
source: Driving kinesins slow down and resisting kinesins speed up to ~830 nm/s, which is the average microtubule velocity (taken from the velocity statistics discussed later in Figure 4C).
evidence: This is experimental data from velocity analysis.

claim: Individual kinesin duration and run length decreases by 2-to-3-fold when kinesin surface concentration increases from 0.03 to 0.46 kinesin/µm2.
source: Figure 3F shows that individual kinesin duration and run length decreases by 2-to-3-fold when kinesin surface concentration increases from 0.03 to 0.46 kinesin/µm2 (~16 fold increase in surface concentration).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Negative cooperativity of kinesins can be explained by the shorter run length of each participating kinesin.
source: Thus, using a force-gliding assay, we find that negative cooperativity of kinesins can be explained by the shorter run length of each participating kinesin.
evidence: This is an inference/conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Multiple kinesins can rescue a microtubule decorated with a QD as roadblock by detaching from the microtubule a kinesin stuck at a roadblock, and then collectively guiding the microtubule forward.
source: With the force-gliding assay, we can now observe multiple kinesins rescue a microtubule decorated with a QD as roadblock. The multiple kinesins do this by detaching from the microtubule a kinesin stuck at a roadblock, and then collectively guiding the microtubule forward.
evidence: This is experimental observation from the force-gliding assay with roadblocks.

claim: As the roadblock concentration increases from 0 to 30 to 100 nM, the proportion of stuck microtubule increases from 7% to 12% to 29%.
source: As the roadblock concentration increases from 0 to 30 to 100 nM, the proportion of stuck microtubule increases from 7% to 12% to 29%.
evidence: This is experimental data from roadblock experiments.

claim: The average velocity of the fast microtubules decreases from 926 nm/sec to 857 nm/sec to 806 nm/sec as roadblock concentration increases.
source: The average velocity of the fast microtubules also decreases from 926 nm/sec to 857 nm/sec to 806 nm/sec, consistent with previous roadblock studies (Chaudhary et al., 2018).
evidence: This is experimental data from roadblock experiments, consistent with cited literature.

claim: As the number of kinesin increases from 1 to 2–3 to 4–5, the proportion of stuck microtubules decreases from 35% to 31% to 13%.
source: Here, as the number of kinesin increases from 1 to 2–3 to 4–5, the proportion of stuck microtubules decreases from 35% to 31% to 13%, respectively, and eventually to zero when there are 6–8 kinesin moving the microtubule.
evidence: This is experimental data from roadblock experiments with varying kinesin numbers.

claim: The proportion of stuck microtubules eventually reaches zero when there are 6–8 kinesin moving the microtubule.
source: Here, as the number of kinesin increases from 1 to 2–3 to 4–5, the proportion of stuck microtubules decreases from 35% to 31% to 13%, respectively, and eventually to zero when there are 6–8 kinesin moving the microtubule.
evidence: This is experimental data from roadblock experiments with varying kinesin numbers.

claim: The velocities of fast microtubules remain constant at around 805 nm/s regardless of motor number.
source: The velocities of fast microtubules remain constant at around 805 nm/s regardless of motor number.
evidence: This is experimental data from roadblock experiments with varying kinesin numbers.

claim: Roadblock-induced pauses can be reduced, eventually to nearly zero, by having more motors available to drive the cargo.
source: This shows that roadblock-induced pauses can be reduced, eventually to nearly zero, by having more motors available to drive the cargo.
evidence: This is an inference/conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Half of the tethers ruptured at 30 pN at 10 nm/sec loading rate.
source: We pulled the dsDNAs at 10 nm/sec and 100 nm/sec loading rates (see Figure 5—figure supplement 2 for rationale) and found half of the tethers ruptured at 30 and > 45 pN, respectively (Figure 5C; Appendix 5).
evidence: This is experimental data from optical trap experiments.

claim: Half of the tethers ruptured at > 45 pN at 100 nm/sec loading rate.
source: We pulled the dsDNAs at 10 nm/sec and 100 nm/sec loading rates (see Figure 5—figure supplement 2 for rationale) and found half of the tethers ruptured at 30 and > 45 pN, respectively (Figure 5C; Appendix 5).
evidence: This is experimental data from optical trap experiments.

claim: The few (~4) driving kinesins observed pulling on the detaching kinesin may exert additive forces beyond what a single kinesin can exert.
source: Hence, the few (~4) driving kinesins observed pulling on the detaching kinesin may exert additive forces beyond what a single kinesin can exert.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing experimental observations to optical trap data.

claim: Kinesins dynamically switch their states from driving to resisting and vice versa.
source: We found that underneath the seemingly smooth transport of a microtubule cargo, like that shown in Figure 2B2, multiple kinesins attached and detached frequently, switching their states from driving to resisting and vice versa (Figure 2B3).
evidence: This is experimental observation from the force-gliding assay.

claim: Driving kinesin dwells longer than resisting kinesin on the microtubule.
source: Driving kinesin dwells longer than resisting kinesin on the microtubule, and will slow down under hindering load caused by tension between kinesins.
evidence: This is experimental observation from the force-gliding assay.

claim: Driving kinesin will slow down under hindering load caused by tension between kinesins.
source: Driving kinesin dwells longer than resisting kinesin on the microtubule, and will slow down under hindering load caused by tension between kinesins.
evidence: This is experimental observation from the force-gliding assay.

claim: Tension allows kinesins to communicate with one another.
source: This tension is key in multiple motor transport, and our assay is the first experimental assay to show its presence between motors. Tension allows kinesins to communicate with one another: driving kinesin feels the tug of resisting kinesin and vice versa through this tension.
evidence: This is an interpretation/inference from the experimental observations.

claim: The tensions between kinesins vary between 0 to 4 pN in the force-gliding assay.
source: In our assay, we show that the tensions between kinesins vary between 0 to 4 pN.
evidence: This is experimental data from the force-gliding assay.

claim: In cells, where shorter and stiffer linkers (adaptor proteins) are employed, the tension will likely increase.
source: Since our assay uses a long and flexible linker (1565-base pair DNA), we therefore predict that in cells, where shorter and stiffer linkers (adaptor proteins) are employed, the tension will likely increase.
evidence: This is a prediction/speculation based on the experimental findings and reasoning about cellular conditions.

claim: Arpağ et al. found that the tension in their simulation varies between 0 to 10 pN for driving kinesin and 0 to 15 pN for resisting kinesin.
source: Arpağ et al. found that the tension in their simulation varies between 0 to 10 pN for driving kinesin and 0 to 15 pN for resisting kinesin (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), larger than the 0 to 4 pN tension measured in our system.
evidence: This is a comparison to simulation results from cited literature.

claim: Arpağ et al. predicted that one-third of the driving/resisting kinesins will be resisting.
source: In fact, Arpağ et al. predicted that one-third of the driving/resisting kinesins will be resisting (Figure 5—figure supplement 4) (Arpağ et al., 2014), similar to the result of our measurement.
evidence: This is a comparison to simulation results from cited literature.

claim: Membrane fluidity will reduce the tension between the kinesins.
source: Nevertheless, we predict that membrane fluidity will reduce the tension between the kinesins, though the ratio between driving and resisting kinesins will likely remain the same.
evidence: This is a prediction/speculation based on reasoning about cellular conditions.

claim: Grover et al. (2016) found that gliding velocity of microtubules transported by membrane-bound kinesin decreases with increasing membrane fluidity.
source: Grover et al. (2016) found that gliding velocity of microtubules transported by membrane-bound kinesin decreases with increasing membrane fluidity.
evidence: This is a citation to published work.

claim: A team of kinesin motors will travel faster on a fluid vesicle due to the biased detachment of resisting motors.
source: Our study found that resisting kinesin motors will detach faster than driving motors, and we predict that, just like Myosin Va, a team of kinesin motors will travel faster on a fluid vesicle due to the biased detachment of resisting motors.
evidence: This is a prediction/speculation based on the experimental findings and comparison to Myosin Va.

claim: The one-third resisting kinesin fraction (and two-third driving kinesin fraction) is a consequence of the asymmetric run length to load.
source: The one-third resisting kinesin fraction (and two-third driving kinesin fraction) is a consequence of the asymmetric run length to load, since resisting kinesin detaches faster than driving kinesin at the same force.
evidence: This is an inference/explanation based on the experimental observations.

claim: A 33% resisting kinesin strategy is a strategy that balances the drag and run length.
source: Since 0% resisting kinesin has low drag and short run length, while 50% resisting kinesin has high drag and long run length, we hypothesize that a 33% resisting kinesin strategy is a strategy that balances the drag and run length.
evidence: This is a hypothesis/speculation based on reasoning about the experimental findings.

claim: When kinesin surface concentration is increased 16-fold, there is only a 2-fold increase in the total number of kinesins driving and resisting the microtubule.
source: With force gliding assay, we are able to directly observe that when kinesin surface concentration is increased 16-fold, there is only a 2-fold increase in the total number of kinesins driving and resisting the microtubule (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Negative cooperativity arises because the run length and binding duration of driving and resisting kinesins decrease as more kinesins participate in transport.
source: Furthermore, we find that this negative cooperativity arise because the run length and binding duration of driving and resisting kinesins decrease as more kinesins participate in transport (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an inference/explanation based on experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: When one kinesin is stuck on a roadblock on a microtubule, other kinesins combine forces to help detach the stuck kinesin.
source: In our assay, probing the effect of roadblocks on multiple motor cargo transport, we found that when one kinesin is stuck on a roadblock on a microtubule, other kinesins combine forces to help detach the stuck kinesin (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is experimental observation from roadblock experiments.

claim: Having more kinesins on the cargo leads to smoother cargo velocity and reduction of stuck cargo events.
source: As a result, having more kinesins on the cargo leads to smoother cargo velocity and reduction of stuck cargo events (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is experimental observation from roadblock experiments.

claim: Kinesins can augment their forces in the presence of roadblocks.
source: Using an optical trap, we indirectly quantified the force in the system and concluded that kinesins can augment their forces in the presence of roadblocks and, thus, can help in overcoming the roadblocks (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from optical trap experiments.

claim: The average transition rate of a single kinesin is 4.9 transitions/min.
source: The average transition rate of a single kinesin is 4.9 transitions/min (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The majority (52%) of transitions are drive-to-drive transitions.
source: The majority (52%) of these transitions are drive-to-drive transitions, during which kinesin drives, then return to equilibrium while still being attached to or after detaching from the microtubule, and then drives again.
evidence: This is experimental data from transition analysis.

claim: The drive-to-resist transitions and resist-to-drive percentage contribute 16% of all transitions each.
source: The drive-to-resist transitions and resist-to-drive percentage contribute 16% of all transitions each.
evidence: This is experimental data from transition analysis.

claim: Kinesins are constantly changing roles between driving and resisting.
source: This shows the highly dynamic nature of kinesin working in a team. Rather than one kinesin taking the lead all the time, kinesins are constantly changing roles between driving and resisting.
evidence: This is an inference/conclusion drawn from the transition data.

claim: The average force exerted by driving/resisting kinesin over time increases from less than ~1 pN when it first binds (t < ~0.8 s) to ~3-4 pN at ~5 sec.
source: A total of 1478 driving kinesins and 573 resisting kinesins was used. Before 0.8 s, which is the time for dsDNA to stretch near its contour length, assuming a kinesin velocity of 800 nm/s, the tension is on average less than ~0.4 pN. After 0.8 s, the tension increases and stays between below ~4 pN until kinesin detaches.
evidence: This is experimental data from force analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The force results are in semi-quantitative agreement with the result of Milic et al.
source: Consequently, our results of 0–4 pN tension between driving and resisting kinesins are in semi-quantitative agreement with the result of Milic et al.
evidence: This is a comparison of the authors' results to published literature.

claim: Velocity asymmetry can be observed in individual driving and resisting traces that are involved in multiple kinesin transport.
source: Overall, we show that velocity asymmetry can be observed in individual driving and resisting traces that are involved in multiple kinesin transport.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental observations.

claim: Velocity asymmetry leads to resisting and driving kinesins speeding up or slowing down, respectively, to match the velocity to the cargo speed.
source: Such velocity asymmetry leads to resisting and driving kinesins speeding up or slowing down, respectively, to match the velocity to the cargo speed.
evidence: This is an inference/conclusion drawn from the velocity data.

claim: 18 examples were found in which a microtubule is stuck at a kinesin and is rescued by the action of other kinesins.
source: After scanning through our entire dataset, we found 18 similar examples in which a microtubule is stuck at a kinesin and is rescued by the action of other kinesins.
evidence: This is a count of observed events in the experimental dataset.

claim: Nine instances were observed when a resisting kinesin is stuck at a roadblock while other kinesins keep driving the microtubule, causing the stuck kinesin to detach from the surface.
source: In support of the hypothesis that more motors help cargos overcome roadblocks and reduce cargo pauses, we observed nine instances when a resisting kinesin is stuck at a roadblock while other kinesins keep driving the microtubule, causing the stuck kinesin to detach from the surface.
